data: What questions do you have for the Government on the draft PWS? Please identify the specific section(s) if applicable.
Please provide one relevant example of your company performing FedRAMP package review or comparable cloud security engineering work.

Please describe the labor mix needed to support FedRAMP 20x from end-to-end package reviews. Please identify which activities require senior engineering judgment and the qualifications or experience you would recommend for each role.
Before beginning a review, how would you identify organizational conflicts of interest involving your company, affiliates, employees, or subcontractors?

Please explain how your personnel would determine whether a provider has adequately demonstrated a Key Security Indicator (KSI). Please distinguish among a security assertion, a security measure, evidence of implementation, evidence of effectiveness, verification, validation, and independent verification and validation. Please provide one concise example demonstrating these distinctions.

Please describe how your personnel would review a FedRAMP 20x Security Decision Record for completeness, technical sufficiency, consistency, and traceability. Please identify the evidence reviewers would expect and the conditions that would result in a question, finding, escalation, or recommendation that the package is not ready to proceed.
How quickly could your team begin supporting active reviews, and how would you handle changes to FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures during performance?

Is there sufficient expert staffing available in the Washington DC metro area to support on-site requirements with the FedRAMP team at GSA, or is remote staffing outside the DC metro area necessary to maintain the highest quality of contractor staff?
How quickly could your team begin supporting active reviews, and how would you handle changes to FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures during performance?

Proposed starts range from immediate support to phased mobilization over several weeks. Some timelines begin at award; others begin after access, screening, or onboarding. Many answers describe version tracking, updated procedures, testing, and Government direction when rules or tools change.
[Noblis](s13) describes day-one incumbent support; [Longevity](s12) targets five business days after prerequisites; [WITS](s17) targets supervised review in 45 days and full capacity in 90.
[Coretec](s11) describes rechecking in-flight packages; [Excentium](s16) describes retaining the governing baseline unless directed otherwise.
[Cloud9](s05), [Softthink](s06), and [EY](s31) include testing revised tools or checks.

We can put a lead and a first review pod in place within 30 days of award. We reach full strength by day 60, if GSA access approvals keep pace. We would overlap the current task order before it ends on 01/29/2027. No package stalls in the handoff.

Rules change often in 20x. We plan for it in four steps.
1. Watch. One person tracks each FedRAMP rule, schema, and process release. Example: on 10/08/2026, Class B historical metrics moved from MUST to SHOULD.
2. Assess. Within 2 business days, we tell the Task Lead what changed and which packages it hits.
3. Update. Once the Government approves, we update checklists, job aids, and test scripts.
4. Tag. Each review records the rule set it used. Packages in flight stay tied to the right rules.
Like [Obsidian](s35), targets reviews in 30 days and full strength in 60, with two-business-day change-impact notes.

Armavel can begin supporting active reviews immediately upon award, contingent on completion of Government-directed onboarding, access provisioning, and assignment of review priorities. Our transition lead will confirm the active queue, assignments, dependencies, and deadlines; receive knowledge transfer; and establish intake, status tracking, escalation, and quality control. We will phase qualified cybersecurity, cloud-security, and authorization personnel into priority work while building full operational capability.

When FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures change, we will assess impacts on in-flight reviews, evidence, automated validations, schedules, and staffing, then provide risks and implementation options to the Government. Upon direction, we will update procedures, checklists, templates, workflows, and traceability records; reprioritize affected work; validate revised machine-readable artifacts with Government-approved tools; and report status and constraints. Final policy interpretations, risk determinations, and package decisions remain with authorized Government officials.
Like [Life Cycle Engineering](s02), describes immediate support after prerequisites; proposes phased capacity and Government options for change impacts.

Assurit can name its Task Lead and Technical Lead at award, begin supervised review of active packages within 30 days of receiving Government access, and reach full capacity within 60–90 days. During the first 30 days, staff complete GSA onboarding, learn the PMO's SOPs and tools, and shadow active reviews. Senior reviewers check all early work before release. The main dependencies are GSA suitability and PIV processing, access to package repositories and ticketing systems, and hand-off of the current SOP. Our transition-in plan tracks each one. We manage rule, schema, and procedure changes as versioned configuration. We monitor the FedRAMP rules repository, changelog, RFCs, and schema releases, and analyze each change against open packages and review checklists. Checklists and validation scripts are versioned to each rule and schema release. After Government approval we update job aids within five business days and brief reviewers. For packages already in review, we apply the version the Government directs, record which version was used, and assess each change's impact on open findings.
Like [Quzara](s25), targets supervised reviews in 30 days and full capacity in 60–90; starts its review clock after access.

Start: Cloud9 can place a core team (Task Lead, FedRAMP Technical Lead, two reviewers) within 30 days of award, beginning active reviews as soon as the Government grants system access and interim suitability. The full team reaches operational capability within 60 to 90 days, with a transition overlap alongside the incumbent.

Changes: Cloud9 tracks the FedRAMP rules, KSI, schema and changelog releases each week. For each change, Cloud9 delivers an impact note within 5 business days: what changed, affected checklists, scripts and packages in review, and a recommended effective date. Updated checklists, job aids and validation scripts stay under version control, are tested against sample packages, and go into use only after Government approval. Packages in review follow the rule version the Government designates. Reviewers are briefed before each change takes effect. Cloud9 already does this at DOC/NTIS, where it updates policies, procedures and its 20+ SOPs whenever systems, regulations or policies change, and it supported NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 transitions for Sona Systems and Treasury OIG (as subcontractor).
Like [Deloitte](s30), targets a 30-day core and full capacity in 60–90 days; tests revised scripts against sample packages.

Our core review team, led by Program Lead [personal name removed] (20 years federal cyber program delivery, DISA's managed security program for 600 organizations, direct FedRAMP PMO coordination), FedRAMP Lead [personal name removed] (30+ years, currently owns FedRAMP High authorization and Security Decision Record review for a multi-cloud SaaS platform), and the other named leads already hold required certifications and FedRAMP-aligned experience. They start transition-in day one and support active reviews within 10 business days of receiving GSA access and screening, inheriting the incumbent's open packages and trackers in week one. A cleared FedRAMP-experienced bench fills any gap.
For rule, schema, or procedure changes during performance, our FedRAMP Lead monitors FedRAMP PMO guidance and KSI updates, our Automation Lead updates validation scripts and schemas, and our Task Lead issues a controlled change notice with updated checklists before the change applies. Every package in flight is rechecked against the new version and the Government Task Lead is told which open findings are affected. Changes are logged and version controlled.
Like [Softthink](s06), targets reviews within ten business days after access; describes rechecking every in-flight package against new versions.

CVP could begin supporting reviews within two weeks of contract award, utilizing  incumbent knowledge, existing cleared personnel, and an established transition methodology from USDA FSIS ISSP II experience. Key Personnel would be on-site and ready with full team mobilization completed by Day Fourteen. CVP would use the transition period to onboard GFI, establish review workflows, and confirm OCI screenings for all assigned personnel, per PWS Section 9.0 requirements. To handle changes to FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures during performance, CVP would maintain a designated Change Intelligence function within our Task Lead role, monitoring FedRAMP PMO communications, OSCAL schema repositories, and Federal Register updates. Upon identification of a rule or schema change, CVP would conduct an immediate impact assessment, update internal review checklists and templates, brief all reviewers within 48 hours, and document process changes per PWS Section 3.7. CVP's FSIS experience adapting to evolving NIST guidelines, OMB mandates, and USDA policy changes mid-contract demonstrates our ability to absorb procedural changes without disrupting delivery timelines or quality standards.
Targets reviews and full mobilization within two weeks, while [Secured IT Solutions](s04) separates an initial cell from capacity by day 45.

CMIC can field an initial DC-based core team within 21 days of award and support supervised reviews within 45 days, assuming timely suitability/PIV processing, GFE, and access to package repositories and validation tools, which are the main schedule dependencies. Our transition-in plan covers onboarding, SOP familiarization, shadowing incumbent or Government reviewers, supervised reviews, and full operational capability. 

For changes to FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures, we would monitor Government  issued updates, record effective dates and affected criteria, and assess impacts to review checklists, data mappings, validation procedures, templates, and work in progress. We would brief personnel, update controlled procedures and training, and document transition treatment for packages already under review. For machine-readable changes, we would test updates using Government approved tools and sample data where authorized, record validation limitations, and elevate ambiguities for Government direction rather than independently interpret policy.
Like [WITS](s17), targets supervised reviews in 45 days; proposes a DC core in 21 days, subject to access.

Yes. The DC-Baltimore corridor has a deep pool of FedRAMP, agency A&A and cloud security talent, including staff who have supported FedRAMP, CISA, DHS and DoD authorization programs. CSD is headquartered in Baltimore, MD, within daily commuting distance of GSA headquarters. We recommend a hybrid model: a DC-area core (Technical Lead, QA Reviewer, Task Lead and a share of reviewers) available on-site at the Director's discretion, with remote reviewers allowed for the most specialized roles, such as automation and data engineering. Requiring all staff to be DC-local is feasible but narrows the pool for scarce skills and may raise labor rates. Clear telework, device and data-handling rules in the final PWS would let remote staff work securely in Government-approved systems.
This cell describes local and remote staffing, whereas [ACE](s01) and other answers describe start dates and handling changes.

Mobilization Timeline: CyberStorm Defense can fully mobilize and begin executing active FedRAMP 20x reviews within 5 to 10 business days of award. Operating via our active GSA MAS contract (SINs 54151HACS, 518210C, 54151S) with pre-screened engineering talent holding active Public Trust and clearance-ready suitability eliminates administrative and staffing bottlenecks.   Handling Rule & Schema Changes: CSD maintains an agile engineering and compliance framework. When FedRAMP updates assessment rules, OSCAL schemas, or validation procedures, our internal automation pipelines and parsing harnesses are updated within rapid sprint cycles (typically 48–72 hours). Lead assessors participate in continuous technical synchronization to update assessment templates, ensuring zero disruption to active federal package reviews.
Targets full mobilization in five to ten business days, while [Navira](s18) uses ten business days for leads and later milestones for the full team.

CybertLabs can target initial support for active reviews within 10 business days of authorization to proceed, contingent on Government onboarding, required access, and package availability. Our FedRAMP practice would deploy an initial technical lead and qualified reviewers, complete conflict screening, align with Government procedures, and confirm readiness through a calibrated package review. Additional engineering, automation, NIST RMF, and QA resources would scale with workload.
We would manage changes through a controlled process: monitor Government-issued updates; assess impacts on active packages, evidence requirements, validation tools, and schedules; and obtain Government direction on applicability and transition dates. Version-controlled review criteria, schemas, scripts, and checklists would preserve the baseline used for each package. Before adopting changes, we would test affected validation tools, brief reviewers, and calibrate interpretations with the Government. We would document affected findings, perform targeted re-review where directed, and flag schedule or risk impacts promptly. Government officials retain policy interpretation authority.
Like [Coretec](s11), targets initial reviews within ten business days after authorization-related prerequisites; includes calibrated review.

Deloitte can begin supporting active reviews within 30 days of award. An initial adequate group of pre-identified and screened reviewers starts on day one, and a bench of adequate vetted engineers brings us to full strength in 60-90 days. Our transition-in plan covers staffing, onboarding, access, knowledge transfer, and shadowing of in-flight reviews, so reviewers work to Government procedures from the first package. 

FedRAMP 20x is evolving quickly, and our process is built for it. We track FedRAMP public notices, requests for comment, the rules changelog, and schema releases on a set cadence. A rules-and-schema lead assesses each change within 3-5 business days (based on the scale of change) and tells the Government Task Lead what it means for reviewers, schedules, and quality. Review sheets, checklists, validation scripts, and training are version-controlled and updated only with Government approval; reviewers get short job aids and calibration sessions; and in-flight packages are reviewed against the rule version the Government designates. Lessons learned feed back into process documentation.
Like [Cloud9](s05), targets reviews in 30 days and full strength in 60–90; adds three-to-five-day change assessments.

Devis could begin once Government access and onboarding are complete (PWS 12.0); start timing depends on access approvals. On our prior State Department program, Devis cut time to hire to 30 days for candidates already holding a clearance. To handle rule, schema, and procedure changes, every review checklist, validation script, and template would carry the rule or schema version it applies to. The Technical Lead tracks the FedRAMP 2026 rules changelog and machine-readable rules repository and logs each change with its effective date and grace period (ongoing certification under the 2026 rules starts 2027-01-01), the data engineer updates validation against the new schema, reviewers receive a short briefing, and in-flight packages are flagged for the version they were submitted under so findings stay consistent. Changes take effect only on Government approval.
Like [IBSS](s22), starts after access and onboarding; records review-tool versions and the submitted version of in-flight packages.

EY could begin supporting active reviews within days of award, mobilizing existing federal cyber staff once GSA confirms screening, access, and dependencies. EY would complete knowledge transfer, train reviewers on 20x rules, KSIs, and schemas, calibrate them on GSA examples, and apply independent QA through a controlled start before full production. A pooled queue, tiered staffing, our US-based Service Delivery Center, and SI-assisted routine checks let EY scale with volume without reducing attention to detail. As the prime on GSA EVS, EY scaled the workforce quickly to address GSA's backlog of 250,000+ validation requests.
A central governance function would track FedRAMP RFCs, the changelog, and schema releases so changes are ready before their effective dates. For each change, EY would assess impacts, version procedures and validation logic, regression-test tools, and retrain reviewers, applying one interpretation across reviews. In-flight packages would follow FedRAMP's effective dates and grace periods. GSA would approve changes affecting interpretation on authority. Bounded pilots, human oversight, and fallback procedures would govern SI changes.
Like [Softthink](s06), proposes an early start once dependencies are confirmed and tests changes; also describes pilots and fallback procedures.

We can begin active reviews within 30 days of Notice to Proceed, subject to suitability determinations, PIV Card issuance, GSA system and package access, and approved assignments and tools. Days 1-10: confirm OCI screens, staff, access, backlog, and SOPs. Days 11-20: calibrate reviewers on an approved sample and exercise QA. Days 21-30: begin assigned reviews and report open dependencies. The Program Manager then runs a weekly queue review and reports monthly metrics on cycle time, rework, and QA results. We have done this before: at Navy BUMED we onboarded 28 Secret-cleared staff in under 30 days, and on Treasury TCloud we managed NDAs, security training, and PIV cards at transition-in.

For changes, we track FedRAMP rule, schema, and procedure releases, including Consolidated Rules updates, and map each to affected packages, checks, templates, and training. With Government approval, packages already in review stay on their governing baseline unless directed otherwise, and each review records the baseline applied. Staff complete refresher training and tool updates before applying a change, and annual competency checks keep the team current.
Like [Deloitte](s30), targets reviews within 30 days; describes retaining an in-flight package’s governing baseline unless directed otherwise.

FITS can begin reviews of packages within 10 - 15 days of being awarded the contract, pending meeting any government requirements for personnel. FITS maintains qualified staff who could begin rolling onto the project effectively on award.
FITS has established a controlled baseline of applicable FedRAMP rules, schemas, procedures, and review tools. FITS has a designated team including a technical lead that monitors official FedRAMP updates, evaluates each change for applicability and effective date, and assesses its impact on open and completed review work.
Following FedRAMP direction, FITS would update checklists, schema validations, templates, and reviewer training. FITS would test changes before use and document the version applied to each package. FITS would maintain a change log, communicate material impacts promptly, and identify reviews requiring additional work.
Targets reviews in ten to fifteen days pending personnel requirements; [Paragon](s24) specifies fifteen business days after Government authorization.

GRAHAM can mobilize qualified personnel immediately upon notice to proceed and staff DC-area on-site requirements. Our established recruiting/onboarding process supports ramp-up within 30 days; the start of independent reviews remains contingent on GSA access, training and approved procedures. We would baseline current KSIs, rules, schemas, templates and active package criteria; log changes; identify affected packages; update version-controlled rule mappings and automation; test on representative data; obtain required GSA approval; brief reviewers; and preserve historical outputs and exceptions. For in-flight reviews, the Task Lead would agree with GSA how revised criteria apply, preventing silent changes in review basis. We propose deploying/adapting USCIS-proven CCI subject to GSA approval; otherwise, we would replicate its automated validation and dashboard workflow on premises using approved systems. CCI supports repeatable checks, while qualified engineers evaluate exceptions and material risks.
Like [LDR](s27), describes immediate mobilization followed by a phased transition; gives a 30-day ramp and makes tool adoption optional.

Guidehouse proposes a phased start: mobilization and transition planning at award, followed by active reviews as soon as designated personnel complete independence screening, required onboarding, system access, and calibration to Government review procedures. We would prioritize an initial technical lead and review cell, then expand capacity against the approved queue. A firm start date and full-capacity milestone would be established after confirming staff availability, access lead times, and incumbent knowledge transfer; we would not assume access on day one.
For rule, schema, or procedure changes, we would maintain a versioned requirements baseline and change log; assess affected packages, evidence, scripts, and schedules; obtain Government direction on applicability and in-flight treatment; update approved checklists and validators; test changes; and brief reviewers before use. Records would identify the version applied and any revalidation. Policy ambiguities and material schedule impacts would be escalated and resolved through bilateral coordination with GSA.
Leaves a firm start date dependent on staffing and access confirmation, while [Vertekal](s10) gives a 30-day initial-review target.

IBSS can begin supporting active reviews once GSA grants system and package-repository access; start time is set by access more than by hiring. IBSS staffs an initial review cell (Task Lead, Senior Cloud Security Engineer, two Package Reviewers, one automation engineer) and fills the remaining roles during transition-in while the cell learns the Government-approved procedures under the Government Task Lead. Changes to FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures are handled through configuration control of the review procedures and checklists themselves (Section 3.7). Each procedure, checklist, and approved validation script is versioned against the FedRAMP release it implements. When FedRAMP publishes a change, the Task Lead logs a change notice, the Senior Lead identifies which open reviews are affected and recommends to the Government Task Lead whether each continues under the prior version or re-baselines, and reviewers are briefed before the approved version takes effect. The review sheet records the version each package was reviewed against, and rework after each change is reported in the Section 3.7 metrics.

Like [RADIX](s21), starts with access and expands from an initial cell; seeks Government direction on rebaselining affected reviews.

KITC anticipates mobilizing qualified cybersecurity and cloud security personnel within 10 business days of contract award or authorization to proceed. Drawing on 19 years of cybersecurity experience and an established pool of federal cloud security professionals, KITC would assign technical leadership and establish package intake, assessment, quality control, and reporting procedures. Active reviews would begin upon completion of GSA-required onboarding and system access.
KITC would designate a technical lead to track changes to FedRAMP 20x rules, Key Security Indicators (KSIs), Security Decision Records (SDRs), schemas, and review procedures. Each change would be assessed for its impact on active packages, evidence requirements, and automated validation checks. KITC would update review criteria, validate revised procedures, brief reviewers, and coordinate implementation with GSA. Version-controlled records and quality checks would maintain consistent, traceable reviews as requirements evolve.
Like [Navira](s18), targets mobilization within ten business days; distinguishes personnel mobilization from reviews after access and onboarding.

LDR can begin supporting active reviews immediately, onboarding in phases or in an initial wave. Our pre-vetted, cleared talent pool identifies qualified staff within 24 to 48 hours and completes onboarding in 5 to 7 days. At the Department of the Interior (DOI), LDR onboarded 40 highly cleared personnel during a 90-day transition with zero schedule slippage, utilizing job shadowing, system inventory reviews, and artifact aggregation, while retaining over 85 percent of incumbent staff. LDR inventoried all in-flight packages, open questions, findings, and action items; logged Federal Government and provider deadlines; assigned handoff owners; and reconciled all tasks with the outgoing team to ensure seamless operational continuity.

Under strict change control governance for evolving Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) rules, schemas, or procedures, LDR will monitor official updates, assess impact, submit Change Requests (CRs) for Government approval, update reviewer job aids, log baseline versions, and perform delta reviews on in-flight packages without schedule delays.
Like [Graham](s20), describes immediate support with phased onboarding; also describes delta reviews when requirements change.

Our team can support active reviews immediately upon award and receipt of required access. We maintain a team of professionals with expertise in FedRAMP, RMF, NIST SP 800-53, security assessments, evidence validation, and authorization package reviews. To address changes in FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures, we will maintain a formal change management process. We continuously monitor FedRAMP guidance, assess impacts to ongoing reviews, update internal procedures and review checklists, and provide targeted training to reviewers. Any affected review criteria, evidence requirements, or deliverables will be updated and communicated to the Government. We would also maintain version control and reassess impacted packages to identify and resolve compliance gaps. Longevity can begin onboarding immediately upon award and targets active reviews within five business days after receiving Government access, approved procedures, and assignments, subject to confirmation of required staffing. We will confirm qualified reviewer availability, identify an appropriate 3PAO partner based on technical requirements and OCI eligibility, establish secure access, and calibrate reviewers on representative packages before production reviews

As the incumbent contractor with 14 years of FedRAMP PMO support, Noblis would provide immediate, uninterrupted support for active reviews from day one. Our team is already embedded with GSA, fully trained on current processes, tools, and standards, eliminating any ramp-up time. Active reviews continue seamlessly without disruption to CSPs or agencies, protecting the FedRAMP SLAs and brand. 
To handle changes in FedRAMP rules, schemas, or procedures, Noblis applies automation as a core capability. Having helped GSA design, test, and implement FedRAMP 20x, our team has deep experience operationalizing policy changes rapidly, automatically updating forms and review sheets to align with frequent updates. Automated workflows enable quick adaptation of templates, validations, and reporting to reflect new requirements, minimizing rework and ensuring consistency. 
We recommend a dedicated Lead Automation role focused on continuous improvement of workflows and efficiency. This role would drive automated processes, enabling the program to scale to thousands of CSPs.
